sources.entry: SysAdvent - Day 6 - No More On-Call Martyrs

summary.name: No More On-Call Martyrs
summary.one_liner: An essay (SysAdvent 2016, Day 6) by Alice Goldfuss arguing that glorifying on-call pain is a toxic culture and that systems should be made self-healing and on-call rotations healthier.
use_cases: Making the case for healthier on-call rotations at work
Reducing alert fatigue and pager noise
Arguing for automating failure recovery instead of paging humans
Reading about sysadmin burnout and career growth
Finding ideas for on-call compensation policies
summary.what_it_does: The essay argues that self-healing, simple systems are a better way to protect uptime than relying on sleep-deprived humans answering pages. It describes the cultural side of on-call, where ops teams take pride in war stories and firefighting, and contrasts this with developers being empowered to build. It lists questions to check whether a team's on-call culture is toxic. It then recommends better monitoring so only actionable alerts page people, limits on alert fatigue (citing the Google SRE book's guidance of more than two pages per 12-hour shift as too many), fair compensation, and putting developers on-call. It also points to the #oncallselfie hashtag and The On-Call Handbook as resources.
notable: Written by Alice Goldfuss, edited by Justin Garrison, as part of SysAdvent 2016 Day 6
Includes a checklist of questions to diagnose a toxic on-call culture
Cites the Google SRE book's guideline of no more than two pages per 12-hour shift
Points to The On-Call Handbook and the #oncallselfie hashtag
caveats: Opinion essay from 2016, not a tool or product, so specifics may be dated
Argues that self-healing systems are an ideal that few companies have reached, so its main fix is partly aspirational
